extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media professionals, fact-checkers, and readers interested in media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards and practices for producing and vetting broadcast/podcast journalism, especially around reporting accuracy, source verification, and corrections. Focuses on editorial responsibilities when theatrical or first-person material is presented as journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic vs theatrical license
rubrics_metrics.description: "What I do is not journalism. The tools of the theater are not the same as the tools of journalism. For this reason, I regret that I allowed THIS AMERICAN LIFE to air an excerpt from my monologue. THIS AMERICAN LIFE is essentially a journalistic - not a theatrical - enterprise, and as such it operates under a different set of rules and expectations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When material is presented as journalism, theatrical license does not apply — producers must treat content under journalistic rules and expectations. Commentary in the piece reinforces this: 'Whatever different license theater has, it’s pretty plain that it surrenders that license when it presents itself as journalism.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough fact-checking before broadcast
rubrics_metrics.description: This American Life said it 'spent a few weeks checking everything' Mike Daisey said, yet later retracted the episode when discrepancies were found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-checking should be rigorous and substantive — not perfunctory. Verify key claims (locations, timelines, numbers of factories/workers, alleged incidents) with primary sources and documentation; a multi-week, superficial check is insufficient if core facts remain unverified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source verification and contactability
rubrics_metrics.description: Daisey told staffers he didn't know how to get in touch with his translator, and gave a different name than he used in the monologue; Marketplace's Rob Schmitz tracked down and interviewed the translator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the identity and contactability of named sources (translators, witnesses). If a contributor cannot provide reliable contact information for their sources or provides inconsistent names, that is a red flag that should prevent airing until resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration with independent records and audits
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple's audits of its suppliers show that an n-hexane poisoning incident occurred in China, but not in Shenzhen where Daisey said he visited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check extraordinary or specific claims against institutional records, audits, or independent documentation. Discrepancies between a storyteller's account and official records must be resolved before presenting the account as factual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial duty to withhold or kill the story when discrepancies persist
rubrics_metrics.description: Ira Glass said the show 'should've killed the story' after Daisey told staffers he didn't know how to contact his translator and gave inconsistent information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and producers have responsibility to withhold or kill pieces if central facts or sources cannot be verified. The presence of unresolved contradictions is sufficient cause to stop publication/broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections, retractions, and audience updates
rubrics_metrics.description: The program retracted the episode; Glass acknowledged 'we never should've put this on the air. In the end, this was our mistake.' A retraction episode will air and stream online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When materially false or unverified content has been published or broadcast, organizations should publicly correct or retract, explain the error, and make the correction as visible as the original content (air retraction, post statement online, notify stations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing the severity of inaccuracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Some falsehoods were small (number of factories visited, number of workers spoken with) while others were large (claim that he met workers poisoned on an iPhone assembly line in the location he visited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between minor errors and major factual fabrications; weigh their impact on the story's core truth and on public trust. Major factual failures demand stronger corrective action (retraction, public accountability) than minor mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accountability in public explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ira Glass and the show issued a press release acknowledging errors and explaining the decision to retract; commentators argued programs owe audiences updates or corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, public explanations of what went wrong, who was responsible, and what steps will be taken to prevent recurrence. Transparency helps restore credibility and fulfills ethical obligations to the audience.
